name: Prophetic medicine

lead: Prophetic medicine is the collection of health advice, remedies and hygiene habits attributed to the Prophet Muhammad in hadith and later compiled by scholars. Its best-known items are honey, black seed (Nigella sativa), olive oil, dates, henna and cupping (hijama).

People who follow it use these everyday ingredients as part of routines for clearer skin, healthy hair and general vitality, so the appearance payoff is indirect and wellness-oriented. Research on individual ingredients such as black seed and honey exists, mostly in laboratory and small clinical settings, while the tradition as a whole has not been tested as a package.

paras: Practitioners typically take black seed or its oil, honey and dates as foods or supplements, use olive oil on skin and hair, apply henna, and sometimes have cupping sessions performed. Many treat it as a religious and cultural practice rather than a cosmetic one, and it is often combined with ordinary medical care.

Ingredients such as honey, olive oil and black seed are common foods, though concentrated black seed products can cause reactions in some people and honey is not suitable for infants. Wet cupping and cautery involve skin damage, burns, scarring or infection risk, and a few traditional items (camel urine) have drawn health-agency warnings. Clinicians and some Muslim scholars note that relying on remedies in place of treatment for serious illness has led to harm.

angle.text: Followers use the tradition's staple ingredients as part of daily grooming and diet, for example olive oil on hair and skin, honey in masks and foods, and black seed oil as a supplement. The appearance benefit is described by proponents as part of overall health rather than a targeted cosmetic effect.

lead: Prophetic medicine (Arabic al-Tibb al-Nabawi) is advice on illness, treatment and hygiene attributed to the Prophet Muhammad in the hadith, together with the manuals later written to organise it. It covers diet, simple remedies, cupping, cautery and prayer, and it is usually distinguished from the wider Islamic medical tradition that drew on Greek humoral theory [1].

Within appearance culture it matters mainly through its everyday ingredients. Honey, black seed oil, olive oil, dates and henna are used by many Muslim and non-Muslim consumers for skin, hair and general health, and the tradition gives them a religious framing. Followers describe the practice as preventive and holistic, with health seen as bound up with moderation and faith [2].

Research touches the tradition mostly ingredient by ingredient. Reviews describe pharmacological activity in Nigella sativa and its constituent thymoquinone, and some authors propose prophetic remedies as adjuncts to conventional treatment [3][4][5]. Critics and clinicians point to the uneven quality of this literature and to cases where clerics or patients delayed standard care [1].

Honey, black seed, olive oil, dates, henna, cupping

paras: Prophetic medicine draws on narrations of the Prophet's sayings, actions and approvals recorded in hadith collections, which Sunni scholars regard as authoritative [2]. Frequently cited reports state that black seed holds healing for every disease except death, that honey is a remedy, and that God sent down a cure for every disease [2][4].

Wikipedia notes that the corpus includes diet, cupping, cautery, simple drugs and prayers but no surgery, and that its manuals were written by religious scholars rather than physicians. Scholars disagree about how much of it is revelation and how much is inherited folk practice [1].

Medieval authors integrated the hadith with Galenic humoral theory. Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya produced one of the most influential treatises, and al-Suyuti divided medicine into traditional, spiritual and preventive categories and wrote on contagion during plague [1][2].

Black seed (Nigella sativa) is the best-known item. Reviews describe a long folk use for skin disorders and report laboratory antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity attributed to thymoquinone [3][4]. Honey, olive oil, dates and henna are used in food, skin and hair care, and miswak twigs for oral hygiene [1].
Cupping (hijama) is also part of the tradition. Wet cupping is promoted by some practitioners for a range of conditions [6], and it leaves circular marks on the skin.

No clinical studies have tested prophetic medicine as a whole. Studies address individual remedies. Reviews of Nigella sativa summarise animal and human work on its pharmacological actions [3][4], and a 2023 review gathered studies of prophetic remedies as adjuncts in blood disorders [5]. A pilot study examined wet cupping in children with thalassemia [7]. Survey research in Saudi Arabia found that consumer use of herbs and supplements stems largely from belief in prophetic medicine [8].

Wikipedia lists camel urine among reported remedies and notes that the WHO has advised against drinking it. It also reports cases during COVID-19 in which some followers made dubious claims and some clerics delayed standard treatment [1]. Cupping is reported to cause bruising, burns and scarring in some cases, with higher risk for fire and wet methods [9]. A concept analysis in nursing literature urges healthcare providers to understand the tradition so they can discuss it with patients [10].

timeline.event: Medical hadith attributed to Muhammad begin circulating and are later compiled [2].
Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya writes a major prophetic medicine compendium [1].
Reviews and commentaries on black seed and COVID-19 circulate [11].
